nodes.id: Subtopic:Environment|Sustainable consumption and production|Minimalist lifestyles|Environmental consciousness_qna_000
nodes.label: Taxonomy
nodes.question: What does historical materialism refer to in the context of environmental and social change studies?
nodes.answer: Historical materialism refers to a materialist conception of history that aids in understanding historical socioecological processes.
nodes.paragraph: As we will elaborate more below, this position allows us to move beyond both na ve positivist and incomplete culture-centered examinations. We aim to advance a critical sustainability science that better fulfills its interdisciplinary and integrative ambitions, identify the ultimate (rather than proximate) drivers of socioecological problems, and provide a basis for moving beyond conven- tional or one-sided solutions. To structure critical sustainability science, we proceed from two critical scientific traditions. First, we draw on the philosophy of science called critical realism (Bhaskar 2013, 2014). As previously suggested by some scholars in the field (Cockburn 2022; Nastar 2023), this provides valuable meta-theoretical scientific tools regarding the ways in which conceptualize the world, i.e., ontology, and how we study and know this, i.e., epistemology, and the related potential for integrating the natural and social dimensions of sustain- ability science. We then elaborate on the need for a rich theory of historical socioecological processes to apply to our study of environmental and social change and call upon historical materialism, or what might be better referred to as a materialist conception of history (Marx and Engels 1998).

nodes.question: What are the affective and cognitive components measured by the EID and NR scales?
nodes.answer: The EID (Environmental Identity) and NR (Nature Relatedness) scales measure the affective and cognitive components of connectedness to nature.
nodes.paragraph: Among these instruments, probably the most outstanding are the INS scale (Inclusion of Nature in Self Scale; Schultz, 2002 ), the NEP scale (New Environmental Paradigm Scale) and its revised version NEP-R (Dunlap et al., 2000 ), the CNS (Connectedness to Nature Scale, Mayer & Frantz, 2004), the NR scale (Nature Relatedness scale, Nisbet et al., 2009 ) and the EID scale (Environmental Identity Clayton, 2003) The INS, NEP, and CNS scales measure the cognitive dimension of connectedness to nature, whereas the 1 3 Journal of Outdoor and Environmental EducationEID and NR measure the construct S affective and cognitive components (Clayton, 2003 ; Nisbet et al., 2009 ). In this study, the INS scale and the NEP-R scale are used to measure the cognitive aspects of the individual S connectedness to nature. The INS scale was formulated to try to measure both the type of environmen - tal concern and person S behaviours, based on the assumption that self-construction incorporates nature. For example, high connectedness would predict pro-ecological behaviours.

nodes.id: Subtopic:Environment|Sustainable consumption and production|Minimalist lifestyles|Environmental consciousness_qna_002
nodes.label: Ethics and regulation
nodes.question: What is the relationship between people's connectedness to nature and their concern for the environment?
nodes.answer: People’s connectedness to nature is positively associated with greater concern and empathy for the environment.
nodes.paragraph: In this context, it is widely accepted that people S connectedness to nature, meaning the extent to which humans see themselves as part of the natural environment, is positively associated with greater concern and empa - thy for nature. Being more connected to nature promotes pro-ecological behaviour, awakening a sense of responsibility and care towards the environment, as well as entailing several other associated benefits, such as people S health, well-being, or hap - piness (Mayer & Frantz, 2004 ; Mayer et al., 2009 ; Schultz, 2001 ). Further research is required on how the connection between nature and people can be improved, since this could be regarded as key to achieving sustainability (Riechers et al., 2021 ). Schultz ( 2002 was one of the first to define the connectedness to nature construct as the extent to which an individual includes nature within his/her cognitive repre - sentation of self (p. 67). Currently, connectedness to nature could be regarded as a very broad construct that encompasses different aspects. According to Tam ( 2013 ), the same concept is referred to in different ways by different authors and, similarly, there are numerous tools to measure connectedness to nature or something concep - tually related (Barragan-Jason et al., 2022 ; Frantz & Mayer, 2014 ).

nodes.answer: The INS scale was formulated by Schultz in 2002, and it aims to measure both the type of environmental concern and a person's behaviors based on the assumption that self-construction incorporates nature.

In this study, the INS scale and the NEP-R scale are used to measure the cognitive aspects of the individual S connectedness to nature. The INS scale was formulated to try to measure both the type of environmen - tal concern and person S behaviours, based on the assumption that self-construction incorporates nature. For example, high connectedness would predict pro-ecological behaviours.

nodes.id: Subtopic:Environment|Sustainable consumption and production|Minimalist lifestyles|Environmental consciousness_qna_004
nodes.label: Facts
nodes.question: What is the NEP-R scale used to measure?
nodes.answer: The NEP-R scale is used to measure ecological awareness and the degree of environmental concern in adult individuals.
nodes.paragraph: And, specifically, among the teaching body and pre-service teachers, who will promote their students contact with nature and future attitudes of respect for it. The NEP-R scale is one of the most widely used instruments to measure ecological awareness and the degree of environmental concern in adult individuals. Environ - mental concern represents the extent to which people are aware of environmental issues and shows their readiness to personally contribute to solving them (Dunlap & Michelson, 2002 ). According to these authors, environmental concern goes beyond the individual S relationship with nature itself; it means understanding the complexi - ties of ecosystems and the impact of humans on the environment, as well as active engagement to preserve and restore it. The NEP-R scale has been widely used at the international level and in different sociodemographic contexts, mainly in European and American countries. Hawcroft and Milfont ( 2010 ) performed a meta-analysis of 69 scientific articles where the NEP scale had been used, drafted in 26 countries around the world, and highlighted that the scale S ecocentric dimension positively correlates with individuals pro-ecological behaviours.

nodes.id: Subtopic:Environment|Sustainable consumption and production|Minimalist lifestyles|Environmental consciousness_qna_005
nodes.label: Analysis
nodes.question: According to Kennedy et al. (2015), what is the relationship between environmental concern, pro-environmental behaviour, and carbon footprint?
nodes.answer: Kennedy et al. (2015) found that there is a positive relationship between environmental concern and pro-environmental behaviour, which in turn can help in reducing one's carbon footprint.

nodes.id: Subtopic:Environment|Sustainable consumption and production|Minimalist lifestyles|Environmental consciousness_qna_006
nodes.label: Analysis
nodes.question: Can you explain the coefficient for Envier? Awareness in the model?
nodes.answer: The positive coefficient for Envier. Awareness indicates that higher levels of environmental awareness have a positive impact on the dependent variable, and this relationship is statistically significant at the 5% level.

nodes.id: Subtopic:Environment|Sustainable consumption and production|Minimalist lifestyles|Environmental consciousness_qna_007
nodes.label: Taxonomy
nodes.question: What does AC refer to in the context of environmental awareness?
nodes.answer: AC refers to believing in the negative impact on the natural environment, highlighting the understanding individuals have about the consequences of their actions on the environment.

nodes.id: Subtopic:Environment|Sustainable consumption and production|Minimalist lifestyles|Environmental consciousness_qna_008
nodes.label: Factual
nodes.question: What is the relationship between awareness of environmental consequences and pro-environmental behaviour according to the VBN theory?
nodes.answer: According to the VBN theory, individuals are more likely to engage in pro-environmental behaviour when they are aware of the environmental consequences of their actions.

nodes.id: Subtopic:Environment|Sustainable consumption and production|Minimalist lifestyles|Environmental consciousness_qna_009
nodes.label: Analysis
nodes.question: How do biosphere values influence individuals' perception and evaluation of information regarding environmental protection?
nodes.answer: Biosphere values lead individuals to consider themselves as spectators judging others' behaviour for environmental protection. This perspective influences their evaluation of external information related to the environment.

nodes.id: Subtopic:Environment|Sustainable consumption and production|Minimalist lifestyles|Environmental consciousness_qna_010
nodes.label: Analysis
nodes.question: What is the relationship between biosphere values and ecological world-view in environmental decision-making?
nodes.answer: Biosphere values, which reflect a concern for the well-being of all forms of life on earth, are associated with environmentalism and influence decision-making by placing ecology at the centre. Individuals with biosphere values feel a moral duty to protect the environment and natural resources, reflecting in their evaluation of external information.

nodes.id: Subtopic:Environment|Sustainable consumption and production|Minimalist lifestyles|Environmental consciousness_qna_011
nodes.label: Analysis
nodes.question: According to the VBN theory, how do believes, such as the new ecological paradigm, AC, and AR, impact individuals' attitudes towards the environment?
nodes.answer: The VBN theory suggests that beliefs form a causal chain that influences individuals' attitudes towards the environment and subsequent pro-environmental behaviour, showing how environmental concern can strongly affect awareness and responsibility to reduce negative impacts like car use.

nodes.id: Subtopic:Environment|Sustainable consumption and production|Minimalist lifestyles|Environmental consciousness_qna_012
nodes.label: Science and tech
nodes.question: How does an individual's ecological world-view influence their recognition of environmental consequences of to the VBN theory?
nodes.answer: An individual's ecological world-view influences their recognition of environmental consequences resulting from their actions, aligning with the principles of the VBN theory and impacting their sense of responsibility towards preventing or exacerbating negative outcomes.

nodes.id: Subtopic:Environment|Sustainable consumption and production|Minimalist lifestyles|Environmental consciousness_qna_013
nodes.label: Taxonomy
nodes.question: What is AR, and how does it relate to individuals' responsibilities in preventing environmental damage?
nodes.answer: AR refers to the belief that individuals or groups are responsible for causing environmental damage or preventing it. It involves a personal sense of responsibility.

nodes.id: Subtopic:Environment|Sustainable consumption and production|Minimalist lifestyles|Environmental consciousness_qna_014
nodes.label: Analysis
nodes.question: How do an individual's underlying values and beliefs impact their awareness of environmental consequences?
nodes.answer: An individual's underlying values and beliefs, particularly their ecological world-view, significantly influence their awareness of the consequences resulting from their actions.

nodes.id: Subtopic:Environment|Sustainable consumption and production|Minimalist lifestyles|Environmental consciousness_qna_015
nodes.label: Analysis
nodes.question: How do biospheric values and altruistic values affect individuals' environmental concerns?
nodes.answer: Biospheric values and altruistic values lead individuals to have a stronger environmental concern due to their awareness of responsibility for the natural environment and resources, respect for other species' rights, and acknowledgment of the negative impact of their actions on other organisms.

nodes.id: Subtopic:Environment|Sustainable consumption and production|Minimalist lifestyles|Environmental consciousness_qna_016
nodes.label: Analysis
nodes.question: How does the value-belief-norm theory explain young travellers' intention to behave pro-environmentally?
nodes.answer: The value-belief-norm theory suggests that individuals who hold pro-environmental values are more likely to develop a sense of responsibility and obligation towards the environment, leading to environmentally friendly behaviour.

nodes.id: Subtopic:Environment|Sustainable consumption and production|Minimalist lifestyles|Environmental consciousness_qna_017
nodes.label: Analysis
nodes.question: How can attitudes towards the environment impact behaviour in Spain?
nodes.answer: Attitudes towards the environment can influence behaviour in Spain by shaping individuals' perceptions, beliefs, and motivations regarding environmental issues, ultimately affecting their actions towards sustainability.

nodes.id: Subtopic:Environment|Sustainable consumption and production|Minimalist lifestyles|Environmental consciousness_qna_018
nodes.label: Factual
nodes.question: What is the role of environmental awareness in the change of behaviour of Brazilian consumers?
nodes.answer: Environmental awareness plays a key role in changing Brazilian consumers, leading them to seek more sustainable consumer practices, such as preference for local, organic and committed companies with social and environmental responsibility.

nodes.id: Subtopic:Environment|Sustainable consumption and production|Minimalist lifestyles|Environmental consciousness_qna_019
nodes.label: Analysis
nodes.question: Why do people act environmentally according to Molluscs and Axeman (2002)?
nodes.answer: According to Molluscs and Axeman, people act environmentally due to factors such as personal beliefs, attitudes, and values that prioritize environmental protection and sustainability.
